claim: The resection of DNA strand with a 5´ end at double-strand breaks is an essential step in recombinational DNA repair.
source: The resection of DNA strand with a 5´ end at double-strand breaks is an essential step in recombinational DNA repair.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about DNA repair mechanisms.

claim: RecJ is a member of DHH family proteins.
source: RecJ, a member of DHH family proteins, is the only 5´ nuclease involved in the RecF recombination pathway.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by structural and sequence analysis throughout the manuscript.

claim: RecJ is the only 5´ nuclease involved in the RecF recombination pathway.
source: RecJ, a member of DHH family proteins, is the only 5´ nuclease involved in the RecF recombination pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by literature citations in the introduction.

claim: A terminal 5´-phosphate-binding pocket above the active site determines the 5´-3´ polarity of the deoxy-exonuclease of RecJ.
source: A terminal 5´-phosphate-binding pocket above the active site determines the 5´-3´ polarity of the deoxy-exonuclease of RecJ
evidence: This is supported by structural data from the crystal structures showing the binding pocket and its role in substrate orientation.

claim: A helical gateway at the entrance to the active site admits ssDNA only.
source: a helical gateway at the entrance to the active site admits ssDNA only
evidence: This is supported by structural observations and biochemical assays showing substrate specificity.

claim: Continuous stacking interactions between protein and nine nucleotides ensure the processive end resection.
source: the continuous stacking interactions between protein and nine nucleotides ensure the processive end resection
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing protein-DNA interactions and mutagenesis studies showing reduced processivity when these interactions are disrupted.

claim: The active site of RecJ in the N-terminal domain contains two divalent cations that coordinate the nucleophilic water.
source: The active site of RecJ in the N-terminal domain contains two divalent cations that coordinate the nucleophilic water.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structures showing two metal ions in the active site.

claim: The ssDNA makes a 180° turn at the scissile phosphate.
source: The ssDNA makes a 180° turn at the scissile phosphate.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure of the RecJ-DNA complex.

claim: The C-terminal domain of RecJ binds the SSB-Ct.
source: The C-terminal domain of RecJ binds the SSB-Ct, which explains how RecJ and SSB work together to efficiently process broken DNA ends for homologous recombination.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data showing the SSB-Ct peptide bound to the C-terminal domain and biochemical assays.

claim: DNA end resection degrades the 5´ strand of a DSB end and is one of the earliest and most important processes in HR repair.
source: DNA end resection degrades the 5´ strand of a DSB end and is one of the earliest and most important processes in HR repair (Symington and Gautier, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Symington and Gautier, 2011.

claim: In bacteria DSBs are predominantly repaired by either the RecBCD or the RecF pathways.
source: In bacteria DSBs are predominantly repaired by either the RecBCD or the RecF pathways.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial DNA repair pathways.

claim: The RecF pathway is highly conserved across eubacteria and shows functional homology in the eukaryotic HR process.
source: Compared with the RecBCD pathway, the RecF pathway is highly conserved across eubacteria and shows functional homology in the eukaryotic HR process.
evidence: This is supported by examples of functional homology provided in the text and citations.

claim: RecA resembles yeast Rad51 protein with regard to the catalysis of DNA strand invasion and change reactions.
source: For example, RecA resembles yeast Rad51 protein with regard to the catalysis of DNA strand invasion and change reactions (Cox and Lehman, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cox and Lehman, 1982.

claim: RecO is capable of annealing single-stranded DNA-binding (SSB) protein-coated ssDNA and facilitates RecA loading.
source: RecO is capable of annealing single-stranded DNA-binding (SSB) protein-coated ssDNA and facilitates RecA loading (Kantake et al., 2002), a property that is shared with the yeast Rad52 protein.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kantake et al., 2002.

claim: The RecF pathway requires RecJ, a 5´-3´ exonuclease, together with RecQ helicase and SSB protein to initiate DSB end resection.
source: In contrast, the RecF pathway requires RecJ, a 5´-3´ exonuclease, together with RecQ helicase and SSB protein to initiate DSB end resection (Courcelle and Hanawalt, 1999; Han et al., 2006; Handa et al., 2009; Morimatsu and Kowalczykowski, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Deinococcus radiodurans is extremely resistant to DNA-damaging agents, such as ionizing radiation, ultraviolet radiation and mitomycin C (MMC).
source: Deinococcus radiodurans is extremely resistant to DNA-damaging agents, such as ionizing radiation, ultraviolet radiation and mitomycin C (MMC).
evidence: This is established knowledge about D. radiodurans.

claim: The robustness of D. radiodurans correlates with its extraordinary DNA repair capabilities, especially DSB repair, which can rebuild a shattered genome within several hours.
source: This robustness correlates with its extraordinary DNA repair capabilities, especially DSB repair, which can rebuild a shattered genome within several hours (Krisko and Radman, 2013; Slade et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Krisko and Radman, 2013 and Slade et al., 2009.

claim: RecBC is naturally absent from D. radiodurans.
source: In contrast to Escherichia coli, RecBC is naturally absent from D. radiodurans, whereas the key components of the RecF pathway are present.
evidence: This is a statement about the genomic composition of D. radiodurans.

claim: Disruption of recF, recO, or recR significantly sensitized D. radiodurans cells to radiation similar as recA mutant.
source: Disruption of recF, recO, or recR significantly sensitized the cells to radiation similar as recA mutant (Bentchikou et al., 2010; Ithurbide et al., 2015; Satoh et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2008), which suggests that the RecF pathway is the dominant HR pathway in D. radiodurans.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: The RecF pathway is the dominant HR pathway in D. radiodurans.
source: Disruption of recF, recO, or recR significantly sensitized the cells to radiation similar as recA mutant (Bentchikou et al., 2010; Ithurbide et al., 2015; Satoh et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2008), which suggests that the RecF pathway is the dominant HR pathway in D. radiodurans.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic studies cited.

claim: RecJ orthologs have been found widespread in most eubacteria and archaea.
source: RecJ orthologs have been found widespread in most eubacteria and archaea (Aravind and Koonin, 1998; Sanchez-Pulido and Ponting, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to bioinformatics studies.

claim: RecJ was firstly identified in E. coli by its effect on recombination that cells lacking both RecBCD and RecJ showed extreme recombination deficiency.
source: RecJ was firstly identified in E. coli by its effect on recombination that cells lacking both RecBCD and RecJ showed extreme recombination deficiency (Lovett and Clark, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lovett and Clark, 1984.

claim: RecJ is involved in ssDNA gap repair, base excision repair and methyl-directed mismatch repair.
source: In addition to HR, RecJ is involved in ssDNA gap repair, base excision repair and methyl-directed mismatch repair (Burdett et al., 2001; Dianov et al., 1994; Lovett and Kolodner, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: RecJ only degrades ssDNA in a 5´-3´ direction but not capable of DNA end digestion with a blunt end or 3´-ssDNA overhang.
source: As a processive nuclease, RecJ only degrades ssDNA in a 5´-3´ direction but not capable of DNA end digestion with a blunt end or 3´-ssDNA overhang (Cheng et al., 2015b; Han et al., 2006; Jiao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to biochemical studies.

claim: RecJ showed 'dRPase' activity to incise abasic sites.
source: Notably, RecJ also showed 'dRPase' activity to incise abasic sites (Dianov et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dianov et al., 1994.

claim: SSB can interact with RecJ and stimulate its DNA binding and nuclease activities.
source: SSB can interact with RecJ and stimulate its DNA binding and nuclease activities (Han et al., 2006; Morimatsu and Kowalczykowski, 2014; Sharma and Rao, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The initiation of DSB end resection by coordinated activities of RecJ and RecQ depends on the nature of the DNA ends.
source: Recently, it has been shown that the initiation of DSB end resection by coordinated activities of RecJ and RecQ depends on the nature of the DNA ends (Morimatsu and Kowalczykowski, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Morimatsu and Kowalczykowski, 2014.

claim: In E. coli, RecJ nuclease alone is capable of digesting DNA with 5´-ssDNA overhang.
source: In E. coli, RecJ nuclease alone is capable of digesting DNA with 5´-ssDNA overhang, whereas RecQ, a 3´-5´ helicase, is required to initiate DNA end resection with a blunt end or 3´-ssDNA overhangs (Morimatsu and Kowalczykowski, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Morimatsu and Kowalczykowski, 2014.

claim: RecQ is required to initiate DNA end resection with a blunt end or 3´-ssDNA overhangs in E. coli.
source: In E. coli, RecJ nuclease alone is capable of digesting DNA with 5´-ssDNA overhang, whereas RecQ, a 3´-5´ helicase, is required to initiate DNA end resection with a blunt end or 3´-ssDNA overhangs (Morimatsu and Kowalczykowski, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Morimatsu and Kowalczykowski, 2014.

claim: The crystal structures of RecJ orthologue from Thermus thermophilus (ttRecJ) have been solved in the absence of substrate DNA.
source: The crystal structures of RecJ orthologue from Thermus thermophilus (ttRecJ) have been solved in the absence of substrate DNA (Wakamatsu et al., 2010; Yamagata et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The structure of ttRecJ reveals an O-shaped molecule, which comprises a novel oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide-binding (OB) fold domain.
source: The structure of ttRecJ reveals an O-shaped molecule, which comprises a novel oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide-binding (OB) fold domain.
evidence: This is based on previously published structural data.

claim: The hole close to the active site in ttRecJ is too narrow to accommodate double-strand DNA (dsDNA), suggesting the ssDNA preference of ttRecJ.
source: The hole close to the active site is too narrow to accommodate double-strand DNA (dsDNA), suggesting the ssDNA preference of ttRecJ.
evidence: This is an inference from structural observations of ttRecJ.

claim: Two catalytic metal ions coordinated by conserved histidine and aspartate residues were observed in the active site of ttRecJ.
source: Two catalytic metal ions coordinated by conserved histidine and aspartate residues were observed in the active site.
evidence: This is based on structural data from ttRecJ.

claim: In the absence of DNA substrate, the conserved loop region of the nuclease core was disordered in ttRecJ.
source: However, in the absence of DNA substrate, the conserved loop region of the nuclease core was disordered.
evidence: This is based on structural observations of ttRecJ.

claim: DHH family proteins can be divided into three subfamilies based on their sequence similarity and domain arrangement.
source: DHH family proteins can be divided into three subfamilies based on their sequence similarity and domain arrangement (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The subfamily 1 group includes RecJ and nanoRNase (RecJ-like protein), a nuclease that degrades short RNA, and has a distinct DHHA1 domain following the DHH domain.
source: The subfamily 1 group includes RecJ and nanoRNase (RecJ-like protein), a nuclease that degrades short RNA, and has a distinct DHHA1 domain following the DHH domain (Srivastav et al., 2014; Wakamatsu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations and sequence analysis.

claim: The DHHA2 domain is present in the subfamily 2 group (e.g., exopolyphosphatase PPX1 and Drosophila Prune protein).
source: In contrast, the DHHA2 domain is present in the subfamily 2 group (e.g., exopolyphosphatase PPX1 and Drosophila Prune protein) (Ugochukwu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ugochukwu et al., 2007.

claim: The subfamily 3 group is defined by the RecJ eukaryotic orthologue CDC45, which has large insertions between the DHH domain and the C-lobe.
source: The subfamily 3 group is defined by the RecJ eukaryotic orthologue CDC45, which has large insertions between the DHH domain and the C-lobe (Krastanova et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Krastanova et al., 2012.

claim: Bacterial RecJ nucleases have an additional OB fold domain next to the nuclease core.
source: Notably, bacterial RecJ nucleases have an additional OB fold domain next to the nuclease core (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and supported by structural data.

claim: drRecJ shares 42% and 32% amino acid identity with ttRecJ and ecRecJ, respectively.
source: drRecJ is conserved within bacteria, which shares 42% and 32% amino acid identity with ttRecJ and ecRecJ, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: drRecJ contains all the seven signature motifs of the RecJ family nucleases, which belongs to the DHH (motifs I-V) domain and the DHHA1 domain (motifs VI and VII).
source: The sequence alignment revealed that drRecJ contains all the seven signature motifs of the RecJ family nucleases, which belongs to the DHH (motifs I-V) domain and the DHHA1 domain (motifs VI and VII) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Compared with ecRecJ, drRecJ has an additional C-terminal domain that is conserved in the Deinococcus-Thermus phylum.
source: Compared with ecRecJ, drRecJ has an additional C-terminal domain that is conserved in the Deinococcus-Thermus phylum (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both Mn2+ and Mg2+ can activate the nuclease activity of drRecJ.
source: In contrast to the degradation of DNA by ecRecJ in a reaction that requires Mg2+, both Mn2+ and Mg2+ can activate the nuclease activity of drRecJ.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The drRecJ activity in a reaction buffer containing 10 µM Mn2+ is substantially higher than that contains 10 mM Mg2+.
source: However, the drRecJ activity in a reaction buffer containing 10 µM Mn2+ is substantially higher than that contains 10 mM Mg2+ (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overwhelming Mg2+ (10 mM) does not affect the nuclease activity when drRecJ is pre-incubated with Mn2+ (0.1 mM), which suggests that Mn2+ ions are employed for drRecJ catalysis.
source: Overwhelming Mg2+ (10 mM) does not affect the nuclease activity when drRecJ is pre-incubated with Mn2+ (0.1 mM), which suggests that Mn2+ ions are employed for drRecJ catalysis.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: drRecJ is able to processively digest ssDNA and DNA with a 5´-ssDNA overhang (14 nt overhang) to a single nucleotide.
source: drRecJ is able to processively digest ssDNA and DNA with a 5´-ssDNA overhang (14 nt overhang) to a single nucleotide (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: drRecJ cannot resect ssRNA or DNA with a blunt end or 3´-ssDNA overhang (6 nt overhang).
source: In contrast, drRecJ cannot resect ssRNA or DNA with a blunt end or 3´-ssDNA overhang (6 nt overhang), which indicates that a free 5´-ssDNA is essential for drRecJ nuclease activity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A free 5´-ssDNA is essential for drRecJ nuclease activity.
source: In contrast, drRecJ cannot resect ssRNA or DNA with a blunt end or 3´-ssDNA overhang (6 nt overhang), which indicates that a free 5´-ssDNA is essential for drRecJ nuclease activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the substrate specificity data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Three types of drRecJ complexes were crystallized: wild-type drRecJ complexed with dTMP (complex I), a catalytic inactive mutant (H160A) RecJ complexed with DNA bearing a 5´-ssDNA overhang (complex II), and the ternary complex of RecJ-ssDNA and the SSB-Ct (complex III).
source: To characterize the RecJ recognition and incision of the DNA substrate, we crystallized three types of drRecJ complexes: wild-type drRecJ complexed with dTMP (complex I), a catalytic inactive mutant (H160A) RecJ complexed with DNA bearing a 5´-ssDNA overhang (complex II), and the ternary complex of RecJ-ssDNA and the SSB-Ct (complex III).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and is supported by the crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: The crystals were grown in the presence of Mn2+ ions and diffracted X-rays to 2.3–2.7 Å resolution.
source: The crystals were grown in the presence of Mn2+ ions and diffracted X-rays to 2.3–2.7 Å resolution.
evidence: This is reported in the crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: drRecJ contains four domains: an N-terminal DHH domain (residues 49–295), a DHHA1 domain (residues 328–424), an OB fold domain (residues 1–48 and residues 425–532), and an extended C-terminal domain (residues 533–705).
source: drRecJ contains four domains: an N-terminal DHH domain (residues 49–295), a DHHA1 domain (residues 328–424), an OB fold domain (residues 1–48 and residues 425–532), and an extended C-terminal domain (residues 533–705; Figure 2A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The DHH domain and DHHA1 domain are interconnected by a long linker α-helix (α15; residues 296–327) to form the nuclease core.
source: The DHH domain and DHHA1 domain are interconnected by a long linker α-helix (α15; residues 296–327) to form the nuclease core, as previously observed for the structure of ttRecJ (Yamagata et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on structural data and comparison with ttRecJ.

claim: The overall structure and conformation of the drRecJ complexes can be virtually superimposed on the ttRecJ (PDB code: 2ZXP) with the rmsd value of 1.937–2.307 Å over 476 Cα atoms.
source: The overall structure and conformation of the drRecJ complexes can be virtually superimposed on the ttRecJ (PDB code: 2ZXP) with the rmsd value of 1.937–2.307 Å over 476 Cα atoms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The β3-α6 loop, which is disordered in the ttRecJ structures, caps the DNA in drRecJ structures.
source: Above the active site, the β3-α6 loop, which is disordered in the ttRecJ structures, caps the DNA (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The C-terminal-most α-helix (α-CT) becomes ordered in all the drRecJ structures.
source: The C-terminal-most α-helix (α-CT) also becomes ordered in all the drRecJ structures (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures.

claim: The nuclease core of drRecJ exhibits a much decreased nuclease activity and processivity on ssDNA compared with wild-type protein.
source: Compared with wild-type protein, the nuclease core of drRecJ exhibits a much decreased nuclease activity and processivity on ssDNA, which indicates that the OB fold domain is critical for substrate DNA binding.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The OB fold domain is critical for substrate DNA binding.
source: Compared with wild-type protein, the nuclease core of drRecJ exhibits a much decreased nuclease activity and processivity on ssDNA, which indicates that the OB fold domain is critical for substrate DNA binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: drRecJ lacking the C-terminal domain (ΔCTD) exhibits reduced nuclease activity.
source: However, drRecJ lacking the C-terminal domain (ΔCTD) also exhibits reduced nuclease activity, which suggests that the C-terminal domain is possibly involved in OB fold domain orientation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The C-terminal domain is possibly involved in OB fold domain orientation.
source: However, drRecJ lacking the C-terminal domain (ΔCTD) also exhibits reduced nuclease activity, which suggests that the C-terminal domain is possibly involved in OB fold domain orientation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the reduced activity of the ΔCTD mutant.

claim: The DHH domain of drRecJ consists of α/β repeats, in which five central parallel β-strands (β2 to β6 in drRecJ) are surrounded by α-helices.
source: As the representative member of the DHH family proteins, the DHH domain of drRecJ consists of α/β repeats, in which five central parallel β-strands (β2 to β6 in drRecJ) are surrounded by α-helices (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The order of the parallel β-strands is 21345, which is shared by all the DHH family proteins.
source: The order of the parallel β-strands is 21345, which is shared by all the DHH family proteins (e.g., NrnA in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) (Uemura et al., 2013; Ugochukwu et al., 2007; Yamagata et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and citations.

claim: The signature DHH residues (motif III) are located at the end of the fourth strand.
source: The signature DHH residues (motif III) are located at the end of the fourth strand.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: The residues at the end of the first and third β-strands and the DHH motif coordinate two catalytic metal ions to form the active site.
source: The residues at the end of the first and third β-strands and the DHH motif coordinate two catalytic metal ions to form the active site (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Both the DHHA1 domain and the DHHA2 domain are structurally similar with a mixed five-stranded central β-sheet surrounded by α-helices.
source: Both the DHHA1 domain and the DHHA2 domain are structurally similar with a mixed five-stranded central β-sheet surrounded by α-helices (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The topologies of the β-strands are different from DHHA1 (12354, ↑↑↓↑↓) and DHHA2 (12345, ↑↓↓↑↓).
source: The topologies of the β-strands, however, are different from DHHA1 (12354, ↑↑↓↑↓) and DHHA2 (12345, ↑↓↓↑↓).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: A positively charged groove between the DHH domain and the DHHA1 domain binds 5 nt 5´-upstream ssDNA.
source: In both complex II and complex III structures, a positively charged groove between the DHH domain and the DHHA1 domain was observed to bind 5 nt 5´-upstream ssDNA in the same manner (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures.

claim: Multiple loops located at the interface between the DHH domain and the DHHA1 domain bind the first two nucleotides.
source: Multiple loops located at the interface between the DHH domain and the DHHA1 domain bind the first two nucleotides (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures.

claim: The helical gateway primarily binds the +3 to +5 nucleotides.
source: In contrast, the helical gateway, which is composed of three α-helices, primarily binds the +3 to +5 nucleotides (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structures shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Ala substitutions of key residues in the helical gateway (Arg280 in α13; Arg313/Arg314 in α15, and Lys353 in α16) reduce the DNA-binding and nuclease activity with multi-stops at 5–7 nt.
source: Ala substitutions of key residues in the helical gateway (Arg280 in α13; Arg313/Arg314 in α15, and Lys353 in α16) reduce the DNA-binding and nuclease activity with multi-stops at 5–7 nt (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), which suggests that the helical gateway is essential for DNA binding and translocation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The helical gateway is essential for DNA binding and translocation.
source: Ala substitutions of key residues in the helical gateway (Arg280 in α13; Arg313/Arg314 in α15, and Lys353 in α16) reduce the DNA-binding and nuclease activity with multi-stops at 5–7 nt (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), which suggests that the helical gateway is essential for DNA binding and translocation.
evidence: This is inferred from mutagenesis data.

claim: Four side chain residues form stacking interactions to the 5´-upstream DNA bases.
source: Notably, four side chain residues form stacking interactions to the 5´-upstream DNA bases (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Tyr114 and Tyr80 (motif I) interact with the +1 base at the active site.
source: Tyr114 and Tyr80 (motif I) interact with the +1 base at the active site.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The substitution of deoxyribose sugar with ribose sugar clashes with the Tyr114 residue, which is consistent with the notion that drRecJ nuclease only acts on DNA.
source: The substitution of deoxyribose sugar with ribose sugar clashes with the Tyr114 residue, which is consistent with the notion that drRecJ nuclease only acts on DNA (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis and substrate specificity data.

claim: Val224 (motif IV) and Phe269 (motif V) insert between the +2/+3 base and +4/+5 base.
source: Val224 (motif IV) and Phe269 (motif V) insert between the +2/+3 base and +4/+5 base.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Ala substitutions of Val224 and Phe269 impair the DNA-binding, nuclease activity and processivity of drRecJ.
source: Ala substitutions of these two residues also impair the DNA-binding, nuclease activity and processivity of drRecJ (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The OB fold domain of drRecJ at the side of the DNA entrance interacts with three downstream nucleotides (+8 to +10).
source: The OB fold domain of drRecJ at the side of the DNA entrance interacts with three downstream nucleotides (+8 to +10; Figure 3A,D).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 3A,D.

claim: The OB fold domain comprises an N-terminal region and a typical OB fold located next to the DHHA1 domain.
source: This domain comprises an N-terminal region and a typical OB fold located next to the DHHA1 domain (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Five β-strands (β13 to β17) in the OB fold are orthogonally located to form a mixed β-barrel with a Greek topology (12354).
source: Five β-strands (β13 to β17) in the OB fold are orthogonally located to form a mixed β-barrel (Figure 4A), which has a Greek topology (12354) that is identical to the topology of other proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Bernstein et al., 2004; Bochkareva et al., 2002; Leiros et al., 2005; Raghunathan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison with other OB fold proteins.

claim: The L2 loop (β14-β15 loop) is short and the top of the β-barrel is capped by an additional α helix in the OB fold of drRecJ.
source: Compared with the canonical OB fold involved in ssDNA binding, the OB fold of drRecJ exhibits certain discrepancies. The L2 loop (β14-β15 loop) is short and the top of the β-barrel is capped by an additional α helix (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The bottom α helix that connects the L3 loop (β15-β16 loop) is absent in drRecJ.
source: Conversely, the bottom α helix that connects the L3 loop (β15-β16 loop) is absent in drRecJ (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Similar structural features were observed in the previously solved drRecO structure.
source: Interestingly, a similar structural features were observed in the previously solved drRecO structure (Leiros et al., 2005) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), suggesting the possible coevolution of the RecF pathway.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with drRecO.

claim: Two conserved aromatic residues, Tyr496 and Trp517 from the L3 and the L4 loop (β16-β17 loop), with residues (Met494, Arg475 and Val477) between the end of the first three β-strands form the downstream DNA-binding surface.
source: Two conserved aromatic residues, Tyr496 and Trp517 from the L3 and the L4 loop (β16-β17 loop), with residues (Met494, Arg475 and Val477) between the end of the first three β-strands form the downstream DNA-binding surface, which interacts with the nucleotide bases (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Ala substitutions of Tyr496, Trp517, Met494, Arg475 and Val477 reduce the nuclease activity of drRecJ on both ssDNA and DNA with 5´-ssDNA overhangs.
source: Ala substitutions of these residues reduce the nuclease activity of drRecJ on both ssDNA and DNA with 5´-ssDNA overhangs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Y496A mutant protein exhibits more severely impaired nuclease activity on DNA bearing 5´-ssDNA overhang compared with ssDNA.
source: Notably, Y496A mutant protein exhibits more severely impaired nuclease activity on DNA bearing 5´-ssDNA overhang compared with ssDNA (Figure 4C), suggesting that the OB fold is critical for the drRecJ resection of DNA with 5´-ssDNA overhang.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The OB fold is critical for the drRecJ resection of DNA with 5´-ssDNA overhang.
source: Notably, Y496A mutant protein exhibits more severely impaired nuclease activity on DNA bearing 5´-ssDNA overhang compared with ssDNA (Figure 4C), suggesting that the OB fold is critical for the drRecJ resection of DNA with 5´-ssDNA overhang.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data.

claim: The C7 base in the 5´-ssDNA overhang of complex II is flipped out into the solvent.
source: Unexpectedly, while drRecJ continuously interacts with the ssDNA (complex III structure, Figure 4B), the C7 base in the 5´-ssDNA overhang of complex II is flipped out into the solvent (Figure 3D and Figure 4B).
